title: Systematic Listing & Trees
coreInsight: Organization turns an informal list of possibilities into a structure that can be checked for completeness and duplication.
targetLearnerRealization: A systematic list or tree makes completeness visible: every allowed continuation has a place, every finished path is counted once, and omissions or duplicates can be detected.
learningObjectives: Build a systematic list or tree by extending every allowed partial choice in a fixed order.
Justify that an enumeration is complete and contains no duplicate outcomes.
Distinguish a decision path from the final object the problem asks to count.

continuity.openingCallback: Reactivate C1's habit of counting complete endpoints, then ask how the endpoints can be organized so none is missed or repeated.
closingSeeds: A large search can be split by a structural feature into complete, non-overlapping cases.
An outcome tree can later become a probability space by marking successful leaves.
Organized categories make it possible to reason about when a future outcome becomes unavoidable.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Any list is systematic if it is long enough.
Seeing a pattern early means the list can stop.
A path of decisions and the final outcome are always identical objects.

beats.purpose: Briefly reactivate C1's endpoint-counting habit using unequal branches before advancing to the reliability of the organization.
beats.expectedRealization: The count comes from five complete paths, not from the number of labels or decision stages.
beats.transitionIn: C1 ended with uneven branches. Warm that idea back up by counting finished plans rather than multiplying automatically.
beats.prompt: How many complete trip plans end at a departure time?

visual.ariaLabel: A trip tree with two bus endpoints and three train endpoints

response.feedback: Count only the endpoints of complete route-and-time paths.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—two bus plans and three train plans make five endpoints.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Follow each branch until it reaches a departure time, then count those finished paths.

steps.body: Bus has 2 endings and Train has 3 endings.

resolution.takeaway: A leaf records a complete path through the choices.

beats.purpose: Let the learner enumerate a small nonuniform choice process before any formal vocabulary or completeness test is supplied.
beats.expectedRealization: The museum has five legal complete routes, but merely finding five route strings does not yet explain why the search is finished.
beats.transitionIn: Counting visible endpoints was easy. Now the endpoints are hidden inside choices that depend on earlier choices—exactly the tangle C1 left us.
beats.transitionOut: Five routes work. The harder question is whether five written lines automatically deserve our trust.
beats.whyNow: A tiny three-stage process has unequal continuations and is small enough for the learner to inspect every complete route.
beats.entryBridge: Write routes in any order you like; use N, S, F, Sp, O, C, and G as abbreviations if useful.
beats.exitBridge: The five found routes answer the question, but the list itself still needs an audit for omissions and repeats.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Complete choice paths written from entrance to finish room.
learnerPrompts: What choices are available after each entrance?
Which labels form one complete route?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes—there are five complete museum routes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your route list. We will organize it next so every branch can be checked.

visual.ariaLabel: Five valid museum routes written in an unsorted order

steps.title: Check each line
steps.body: Each line begins at an entrance, follows an allowed exhibit, and ends in a finish room.

steps.title: Count what was found
steps.body: The list contains five different legal routes.

resolution.takeaway: A list can produce an answer; organization is what will let us certify it.

beats.purpose: Create the need for systematic organization by showing that a list of the correct length can hide both a duplicate and an omission.
beats.expectedRealization: Five written lines need not represent five distinct routes; one duplicate can conceal one missing route.
beats.transitionIn: A classmate also wrote five legal-looking lines. Inspect the records themselves, not just the length of the list.
beats.prompt: Does this list prove that it contains all five distinct museum routes?

visual.ariaLabel: Five museum route records in an unsorted list, available for the learner to inspect

options.text: Yes; five lines always prove five distinct routes.
No; the records themselves must be checked.

feedback.proved: Line count alone cannot detect whether one route was repeated while another was missed.
feedback.not-proved: Right. Inspecting the entries reveals a repeated record and leaves a route unaccounted for.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the list repeats N–F–C and omits S–O–G.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare the first and last entries, then look for the South route ending at the Garden.

visual.ariaLabel: A complete museum route tree with five distinct leaves

steps.title: Find the repeat
steps.body: N–F–C appears twice, so those two lines describe only one route.

steps.title: Find the hole
steps.body: The South–Ocean branch has two finish choices, but the list recorded only Cafe. South–Ocean–Garden was missed.

resolution.takeaway: A duplicate can make a list look long enough while an outcome is still missing.

beats.purpose: Extract the coverage and non-duplication tests from the completed tree in learner language.
beats.expectedRealization: The tree is complete because every partial path has all allowed continuations, and duplicate-free because each decision sequence creates one leaf.
beats.transitionIn: The tree repaired the list. Now identify the features that make the repair trustworthy.
beats.prompt: Which two checks certify this tree? Select both.

visual.ariaLabel: The complete five-leaf museum route tree

options.text: After every partial route, every allowed next choice appears.
Each complete choice sequence reaches exactly one leaf.
Every branch has the same number of leaves.
The diagram happens to show five lines.

response.feedback: Look for one check that prevents omissions and one that prevents repeated paths.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—extend every allowed choice and give each complete sequence one place.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Unequal branches are allowed, and a line count is not proof. Check continuations and unique leaves.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: At North we include Fossils and Space; at South we include Ocean. Every one of those partial routes then shows every allowed finish.

steps.title: No overlap
steps.body: A finished entrance–exhibit–room sequence follows one and only one path through the tree.

resolution.takeaway: A trustworthy organization covers every allowed branch and counts each finished path once.

beats.purpose: Name the method only after the learner has experienced the failure of an unstructured list and the auditability of a tree.
beats.expectedRealization: Systematic listing means using a repeatable order that exposes both coverage and duplication; a tree is one visual form of that method.
beats.transitionIn: You just made the search checkable by giving every next choice a fixed place.
beats.name: Systematic listing and trees
beats.conciseDefinition: A systematic list follows a fixed rule so every allowed outcome appears once. A tree does this by extending each partial choice through all of its allowed next branches.
beats.formalization: Complete = every allowed outcome is represented. Non-overlapping = no outcome is counted in two places.
beats.memoryHook: Open every legal branch; count every leaf once.

beats.purpose: Repair the assumption that decision paths and requested final outcomes are always the same objects.
beats.expectedRealization: The same tree has five routes but only two distinct finish rooms; the question determines what counts as one outcome.
beats.transitionIn: The tree has five leaves because we were counting routes. Change what the question calls an outcome, and the same picture can give a different count.
beats.prompt: If the school records only which room a tour finishes in, how many distinct finish rooms are possible?

visual.ariaLabel: Five museum routes, several of which share Cafe or Garden as a finish room

response.feedback: Ignore how a tour arrived; count distinct final room names.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the only finish rooms are Cafe and Garden.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Five is the number of routes. This question merges routes that end in the same room.

visual.ariaLabel: The five routes grouped into the two distinct finish rooms Cafe and Garden

steps.body: Several decision paths can lead to the same final object. Define one outcome before deciding whether leaves stay separate or merge.

resolution.takeaway: A path is a sequence of decisions; the requested outcome may be that path or something it produces.

beats.purpose: Apply systematic branch extension to the approved authentic path problem, where illegal prefixes must be rejected without hiding unexplored branches.
beats.expectedRealization: Growing every U/D prefix and pruning only when a path goes underground or can no longer balance leaves exactly five valid six-hop sequences.
beats.transitionIn: The museum tree had unequal branches supplied by the rules. In this contest problem, every hop offers U or D, but some branches become illegal while the tree grows.
beats.transitionOut: The five survivors are trustworthy because every U/D continuation was either extended or rejected for a stated reason.
beats.whyNow: The mapped bunny problem turns a short systematic tree into an authentic constrained enumeration and directly tests whether the learner stops only after every branch is accounted for.
beats.entryBridge: Treat each partial hop string as a tree branch. Extend it by U or D unless that next step is already impossible.
beats.exitBridge: Five legal leaves remain: UDUDUD, UDUUDD, UUDDUD, UUDUDD, and UUUDDD.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A branching decision tree whose leaves are complete paths and whose illegal continuations are explicitly rejected.
learnerPrompts: Before listing, what must be true of the total numbers of U and D hops?
Why may a branch be stopped as soon as its running height goes below zero?
At the final animation state, how does each surviving profile correspond to one leaf?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—five six-hop paths return to the ground without ever going below it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your attempt. Extend U/D strings in a fixed order and reject a branch only when it goes underground or cannot finish balanced.

steps.title: Define a legal leaf
steps.body: A complete path has six hops, ends at height 0, and never has a negative running height. Ending at 0 forces three U hops and three D hops.

steps.title: Grow and prune systematically
steps.body: At each legal prefix, consider both next letters. Stop a D branch if it enters the dirt; stop any prefix that cannot still finish with three U's and three D's.

steps.title: Read the surviving leaves
steps.body: The legal leaves are UDUDUD, UDUUDD, UUDDUD, UUDUDD, and UUUDDD.

steps.title: Connection to C1
steps.body: Without restrictions, six two-way stages would create 2⁶ = 64 strings. The systematic tree keeps that structure but removes only branches the rules forbid.

resolution.takeaway: Completeness comes from accounting for every possible continuation—not from stopping when the list looks patterned.

beats.purpose: Separate the reusable enumeration method from the bunny story before independent practice.
beats.expectedRealization: A systematic tree is a ledger of decisions: open every legal next branch, explain every stopped branch, and count complete leaves once.
beats.transitionIn: The bunny paths were harder than the museum routes, but the audit was the same.
beats.heading: The tree is a proof ledger
beats.body: Every partial choice received every allowed continuation. Every stopped branch had a rule-based reason. Every complete sequence occupied one leaf. Those three facts—not the neat drawing—made the count reliable.
math: legal continuations accounted for → complete leaves counted once

beats.purpose: Begin independent evidence with a concise, reusable audit routine.
beats.expectedRealization: The same three questions can guide lists, trees, tables, and path records.
beats.transitionIn: Now use the ledger without a worked branch beside you.
beats.heading: For each count
beats.body: Define one outcome. Choose a fixed order for extending possibilities. Before counting, check that every legal possibility appears and none appears twice.

beats.purpose: Check a near transfer where one forbidden continuation creates an inspectable binary tree.
beats.expectedRealization: Extending A/B strings left to right and refusing BB produces exactly five legal leaves.
beats.transitionIn: Start with a tiny tree: two symbols at each position, with one branch rule.
beats.transitionOut: The five strings are complete because every legal prefix was extended to length three.
beats.whyNow: This isolates systematic left-to-right extension and immediate pruning with only eight unconstrained strings.
beats.entryBridge: Build strings one position at a time and stop only a branch that already ends in BB.
beats.exitBridge: AAA, AAB, ABA, BAA, and BAB are the five legal leaves.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A left-to-right branch tree with forbidden continuations pruned.
learnerPrompts: Did every legal two-symbol prefix receive every allowed third symbol?

visual.ariaLabel: Five legal three-flash strings containing no consecutive B flashes

steps.body: After A, either symbol may follow. After B, only A may follow, because BB is forbidden.
Extending every legal prefix gives five distinct length-three strings.

resolution.takeaway: A forbidden continuation removes a branch, not the obligation to inspect the other branches.

beats.purpose: Check systematic ordering by the most restrictive position rather than by the written order of digits.
beats.expectedRealization: The units digit must be 2, and the tens digit can then be 1 or 3, giving 12 and 32.
beats.transitionIn: A fixed order need not start on the left. Let the strongest rule choose where your list begins.
beats.transitionOut: Starting with the units place made completeness visible in one short branch.
beats.whyNow: The task tests whether the learner chooses an efficient systematic order while preserving the exact outcome definition.
beats.entryBridge: For an even number, decide the units digit first; then extend every legal tens digit.
beats.exitBridge: Only 12 and 32 satisfy both the evenness and no-repeat rules.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A tree whose first branch is chosen by the strongest constraint.
learnerPrompts: Which available digit can occupy the units place of an even number?

visual.ariaLabel: The two even two-digit badges 12 and 32

steps.title: Use the restrictive place
steps.body: Among 1, 2, and 3, only 2 can be the units digit of an even number.

steps.title: Finish the badge
steps.body: No repetition leaves 1 or 3 for the tens digit.

resolution.takeaway: Choose a listing order that makes the restrictions easy to audit.

beats.purpose: Check nonuniform branches and reinforce that designs, not repeated paint names, are the outcomes.
beats.expectedRealization: The same paint color paired with different shapes creates different designs, so the actual branch sizes add to six.
beats.transitionIn: Now branch lengths differ, and the same paint name can appear under more than one shape. Keep complete designs distinct.
beats.transitionOut: Repeated labels were not duplicates because Square–Blue and Triangle–Blue are different shape–paint designs.
beats.whyNow: The problem separates duplicate labels from duplicate outcomes and requires counting the actual endpoints of unequal branches.
beats.entryBridge: Write the shape before the paint so each complete design has one unambiguous record.
beats.exitBridge: Two square designs, one triangle design, and three circle designs make six distinct pairs.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Unequal branches with complete shape–paint outcomes at the leaves.
learnerPrompts: Does Blue under a different shape describe the same design or a different one?

visual.ariaLabel: Six distinct shape and paint designs on unequal tree branches

steps.body: Record both choices. A repeated paint name under a different shape is part of a different complete design.
Count the actual leaves on the three shape branches.

resolution.takeaway: Duplicate checking compares complete outcomes, not isolated labels inside them.

beats.purpose: Check exhaustive listing of all candidate paths before filtering by a geometric constraint.
beats.expectedRealization: All six orders of E,E,N,N are considered exactly once; four hit the forbidden center and two avoid it.
beats.transitionIn: A path constraint now hides inside geometry. Translate each route into a move string so the audit has a fixed language.
beats.transitionOut: The six candidate strings split into two survivors and four rejected paths, leaving no unexamined order.
beats.whyNow: The problem transfers systematic listing from symbolic rules to movement and requires explicit accounting for rejected candidates.
beats.entryBridge: Every route uses two E moves and two N moves. List each order once, then test whether it visits (1,1).
beats.exitBridge: Only EENN and NNEE avoid the center, so two routes remain.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Move strings serving as unique records of geometric paths.
learnerPrompts: How will you know all orders of E,E,N,N have been tested?

visual.ariaLabel: All six orders of two east and two north moves classified by whether they visit the center point

steps.title: List every candidate once
steps.body: The six distinct orders of E,E,N,N are EENN, ENEN, ENNE, NEEN, NENE, and NNEE.

steps.title: Apply the path rule
steps.body: The four strings that begin EN or NE reach (1,1) after two moves. EENN and NNEE do not.

resolution.takeaway: Rejected paths still belong in the audit; give each one a clear reason for rejection.

beats.purpose: Challenge the learner to choose and finish a two-case systematic list under simultaneous composition and endpoint constraints.
beats.expectedRealization: Opposite endpoint colors create two complete starting cases, and each has two legal interior completions.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, two rules act at once. Fix the endpoints first, then finish every branch before counting.
beats.transitionOut: Both endpoint cases were exhausted, so the four-code count is complete rather than pattern-based.
beats.whyNow: The challenge requires an efficient branch order, simultaneous restriction tracking, and explicit completion of all cases.
beats.entryBridge: The first and last symbols must be opposite. Open the R…B and B…R branches, then place the one remaining R.
beats.exitBridge: RRBB, RBRB, BRBR, and BBRR are the four legal codes.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A two-case tree whose leaves are complete constrained strings.
learnerPrompts: After fixing opposite endpoints, how many R symbols remain for the two middle positions?

visual.ariaLabel: Four legal sensor codes organized by their opposite endpoint symbols

steps.title: Fix opposite endpoints
steps.body: The endpoints are either R…B or B…R; these cases cover every code and cannot overlap.

steps.title: Complete each case
steps.body: One R is already at an endpoint, so exactly one of the two middle positions must be R. Each endpoint case has two completions.

resolution.takeaway: Finish every branch of the organizing rule before trusting a pattern or total.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the complete method and its correctness tests before creating the need for casework.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable enumeration defines outcomes, uses a fixed extension rule, accounts for every legal or rejected branch, and counts complete records once.
beats.transitionIn: Across routes, strings, designs, and paths, the surface changed but the audit stayed the same.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable systematic enumeration? Select all four.

options.text: Define exactly what one final outcome records.
Use a fixed order for extending choices.
Extend every legal branch and explain every rejected branch.
Stop when the first few entries form a convincing pattern.

response.feedback: A pattern can suggest where to look, but only a complete branch audit proves the count is finished.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—define, order, account, and count once.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep every check that prevents ambiguity, omissions, or duplicates; do not let an early pattern end the audit.

groups.label: 2. Order
choices: Which choice or constraint comes first?

groups.label: 3. Account
choices: Extend or reject every branch with a reason.

visual.ariaLabel: Four checks for a reliable systematic enumeration

resolution.takeaway: Systematic means auditable: every possibility has one place and every missing branch has an explanation.

beats.purpose: Create the need for C4's structural grouping only after consolidating systematic listing.
beats.expectedRealization: When a tree becomes too large to draw leaf by leaf, grouping outcomes by a decisive feature may preserve completeness with less work.
beats.transitionIn: You can now audit a finite tree leaf by leaf. Let the tree grow too wide to draw comfortably.
beats.prompt: Suppose a search has hundreds of leaves, but every outcome has one of a few possible structural features. How could those features organize a complete count without drawing every leaf?
beats.takeaway: Next, we will turn a large search into a few complete, non-overlapping cases.

notes: Draft technique lesson authored with the repository-local mathinking-lesson Skill and the compact C2 context packet.
Generated museum routes create discovery because their small unequal branches expose both omission and duplicate risks before terminology is introduced.
The additional mapped AMC 8 2024 Problem 13 is integrated in its authorized transfer role because its constrained path enumeration directly fits C2 and has an aligned hop-path animation.

The approved best-candidate ID AMC 8 2024 Problem 9 resolves to a marble-ratio problem although its mapping rationale describes tree counting; it is not forced into C2, and the approved mapping remains unchanged.
All declarative visuals reuse existing generic primitives; no lesson-specific renderer behavior was added.
